slides.title: Purpose and method
bullets: The white-cell count gives general quantitative information and helps to detect bacterial, viral or parasitic infection.
Leukocytes are counted under the microscope in a counting chamber or on automatic/semi-automatic electronic counters.

In a Neubauer (or improved Neubauer) chamber it is recommended to count all leukocytes in the whole marked zone (9 mm²); many laboratories count about half of it. The Goryaev chamber was widely used in laboratories of the former USSR.
Red cells are lysed with an acetic acid solution, after which only the leukocytes are counted.

slides.title: Reagent and dilution
bullets: Acetic acid solution: 2% stained with methylene blue (0.38 mL) in the Aripova book, 3% (0.4 mL) in the QVP book; in both, the blood is diluted 1:20 (20 µL of blood).
Keep strictly to the concentration in the laboratory’s instructions: acetic acid above 5% also lyses the leukocytes and lowers the result.

slides.title: Reagent and dilution
bullets: A counting chamber and matching cover glass, stoppered tubes, a 20 µL pipette, a rubber bulb.
A microscope: 10× objective and 10× eyepiece.

slides.title: Procedure
bullets: 1. Pour the acetic acid solution into the tubes and label them with the requisition number.
2. Take 20 µL of capillary blood without bubbles, wipe the pipette outside, check the blood level.
3. Expel the blood into the acid tube (1:20) with a rubber bulb or an automatic pipette (never by mouth) and rinse the pipette three times in the solution.

slides.title: Procedure
bullets: 4. Mix the contents thoroughly for at least a minute (stopper the tube and invert it).
5. Rub the cover glass on until Newton’s rings appear; fill the chamber by touching its edge with the pipette — do not overfill.
6. Leave the chamber for the cells to settle (Aripova: 2 minutes; QVP: at least 1 minute).

slides.title: Counting and calculation
bullets: Count at low magnification (10× objective, 10× eyepiece) with weak light (condenser lowered, diaphragm closed down).
After the red cells are lysed, count the leukocytes in 100 large squares (1600 small ones) of the Goryaev grid.
Cells on the upper and left lines of each square are counted as well.
For the Goryaev chamber with 100 large squares and a 1:20 dilution: X = a × 50 (a = number of leukocytes counted).
Range in the books: 4.0–10.0 × 10^9/L.

slides.title: Counting and calculation
slides.ex: Example (QVP): 100 leukocytes in 1600 small squares → 5000 cells/µL.

slides.title: Sources of error
bullets: Uneven distribution of cells in the chamber is the commonest source of error; the chamber is left to stand before counting and counting over the whole ruled area is advised.
A badly seated cover glass changes the chamber volume and gives a wrong result.
A wrong ratio of blood to acetic acid.

slides.title: Sources of error
bullets: Acetic acid stronger than 5% also lyses the leukocytes and lowers the result.
Leaving the sample for a long time at a temperature above 28 °C.

slides.title: Quality control
bullets: For the counting-chamber method there is little control to compare against, so every step of the test and of standardisation is carried out carefully.
Stabilised blood, special suspensions, haemolysates and fixed smears are used as control materials.

slides.title: Safety
bullets: Treat all specimens as potentially infectious; blood work is done in rubber gloves with a single-use scarifier.
Never draw material into a pipette by mouth; use a rubber bulb.
Do not use glassware with chipped edges.

slides.title: Principle and place of the method
bullets: Sedimentation goes through three phases: first the red cells settle singly and slowly, then they form aggregates and settle fast, in the third phase the aggregates pack down and settling slows and stops.
ESR is not specific to any disease: it is used as a preliminary test and a screening test.

The Aripova book notes that ESR is not specific for finding acute and chronic diseases, is little used today and has been abandoned in many countries: age, pregnancy, the phase of the cycle and anaemia distort the result.

slides.title: Principle and place of the method
bullets: The international committee for standardisation and WHO recommend venous blood, an anticoagulant tube and a graduated vertical tube (the Westergren principle).

slides.title: Two described variants
rows: Capillary from the finger, or venous

slides.title: Procedure
bullets: 1. Take the sodium citrate solution into a tube; add the blood to it at a ratio of 4:1 and mix well.
2. Draw the mixture into the graduated tube up to the 0 mark; check that the lower edge of the blood meniscus is at 0 and that there are no air bubbles.
3. Stand the tube upright in the rack (in the Panchenkov apparatus its lower end rests on rubber and the upper end is closed).

slides.title: Procedure
bullets: 4. Leave the rack for one hour in a quiet place free of vibration and draughts.
5. After one hour measure in millimetres the distance from the 0 mark to the upper edge of the settled red-cell column — the height of the clear plasma layer.
6. Record the result in mm/h.

slides.title: Limitations and errors
bullets: ESR is not suitable when the red-cell count is reduced or the patient is dehydrated.
Physiological factors (age, pregnancy, phase of the menstrual cycle) and anaemia can give a wrong result.
The value may be raised in diseases that change the plasma protein pattern, chronic infection, normal pregnancy, tumours and tuberculosis.
The capillary-blood, 100 mm tube method used in laboratories of the former USSR should, where possible, be revised to meet international standards.

slides.title: Safety
bullets: In the standard method used in many countries blood may be spilled and aerosols may form, which is a considerable biological hazard.
The international committee for standardisation and WHO recommend single-use closed systems for ESR, so that the blood stays enclosed during testing and disposal.

slides.title: White blood cell count (WBC)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood (EDTA, purple-top tube)  ·  Units: ×10⁹/L, /µL

What it is used for: The test helps diagnose or monitor disorders with a high or low WBC: signs of infection (fever, chills, body aches, headache, a wound that is red, has pus or won’t heal, an ongoing cough), inflammation or autoimmune disease; and a disease or medicine that weakens the immune system — if the count gets too low, the provider may adjust treatment. Children may be tested as part of routine screening.

slides.title: White blood cell count (WBC)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Physiology: White blood cells (leukocytes) are part of the immune system: made in the bone marrow and found in the blood and lymph tissue, they travel through the bloodstream and tissues to where they are needed to fight infections and other diseases. There are five major types — neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils and basophils; the WBC measures their total number.

When you get sick, the body makes more white cells to fight bacteria, viruses or other foreign substances, raising the count. Some cancers, HIV (a virus that attacks white cells) and certain medicines such as chemotherapy lower it.

slides.title: White blood cell count (WBC)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Interpreting the result
cols: Causes of leukocytosis (a high WBC) include infection, an inflammatory disease such as rheumatoid arthritis, allergy, leukemia or Hodgkin disease, and tissue damage from a burn or surgery. Smoking, stress, a reaction to a medicine or pregnancy can also raise the count.

Causes of leukopenia (a low WBC) include bone marrow damage from infection, disease or treatments such as chemotherapy, cancers that affect the bone marrow, an autoimmune disorder such as lupus, and HIV.

slides.title: White blood cell count (WBC)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 1/2
bullets: Pre-analytics: No special preparation is needed, but some medicines may need to be stopped before the test, so tell the provider about everything you take. Do not stop any medicine unless the provider says so.
Adults give a sample from a vein. Newborns and young babies have a heel stick; older babies and children give blood from the fingertip or arm.

Per the WHO phlebotomy guidelines, hematology tests use an EDTA tube (usually purple top): EDTA removes calcium by forming calcium salts. The tube needs a full draw and gentle inversion so the blood mixes thoroughly with the additive — poor mixing can give erroneous results. Cap colors may differ by manufacturer.

slides.title: White blood cell count (WBC)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 2/2
bullets: Interferences: Diet, activity level, medicines, having a menstrual period, not drinking enough water and other factors can affect CBC results; an abnormal level does not always mean a condition that needs treatment.

Limitations: A WBC shows whether white cells are too high or too low but cannot confirm a diagnosis; it is usually done with a complete blood count, blood differential, blood smear and/or bone marrow test. The differential shows the amount of each type.

slides.title: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood (tube type per laboratory instructions)

What it is used for: ESR is used with other tests to help diagnose and monitor conditions that cause inflammation, such as arthritis, vasculitis, infections and inflammatory bowel diseases (ulcerative colitis and Crohn’s disease).
It is ordered for symptoms of inflammation: headaches, unexplained fever or weight loss, joint stiffness, neck or shoulder pain, loss of appetite, anemia.

slides.title: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Physiology: Red blood cells normally sink slowly. Inflammation makes them stick together in clumps, which are heavier than single cells and sink faster. Blood is placed in a tall, thin tube and the speed of settling is measured: faster rates mean more inflammation.

slides.title: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Interpreting the result
bullets: High: A high ESR (red cells sank faster than normal) may come from inflammatory conditions such as giant cell arteritis, arthritis, systemic vasculitis, polymyalgia rheumatica, inflammatory bowel disease, kidney disease, infections, rheumatoid arthritis and other autoimmune diseases, heart disease and certain cancers.

Low: A low ESR (red cells sank slower than normal) may be caused by blood disorders such as polycythemia, sickle cell disease or very high leukocytosis, heart failure and certain kidney and liver problems.

slides.title: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 1/2
bullets: Pre-analytics: No special preparation is needed for this test. If other tests are ordered on the same blood sample, fasting (no food or drink) for several hours may be required.

Interferences: Normal ESR varies with age and sex. Pregnancy, the menstrual cycle, aging, obesity, drinking alcohol regularly and exercise can affect results, as can certain medicines and supplements — tell the provider about them.

slides.title: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 2/2
bullets: Limitations: ESR alone cannot diagnose which condition is causing inflammation, and it is possible to have an inflammatory condition with a normal ESR. A C-reactive protein (CRP) test is commonly done with it to provide more information.

slides.title: Example: Counting chamber
bullets: Formula: Cells/µL = cells counted × dilution ÷ (squares counted × area of one square, mm² × chamber depth, mm)
slides.ex: 1 µL = 1 mm³; ×10⁹/L = cells/µL ÷ 1000. WHO example: improved Neubauer, 4 corner squares (1 mm² each), depth 0.1 mm, 1 in 20 dilution, 188 leukocytes → 9.4 × 10⁹/L.
